Thus, in 66% of the hard cases, the model improves upon or departs from the original author-side response. It introduces an unsupported resolution in 6% of cases. Representative case. One example concerns paper proposing density-based uncertainty categorization framework. The reviewer questions both the novelty of the method relative to existing feature-space density approaches and the practical usefulness of the proposed Bnd and IDM categories. The original rebuttal states only that the introduction, figure, and method sections will be revised to clarify the motivation. This response does not establish empirical novelty or demonstrate that the proposed categories provide distinct practical information. Rather than reproducing this clarification-only response, ACTREVIEW-RL recommends controlled comparison with standard feature-space density baseline, an ablation isolating the contribution of the confusion-based component, and an evaluation testing whether the Bnd and IDM categories provide complementary information. The resulting suggestion extends the original rebuttal by proposing concrete evidence needed to substantiate both novelty and practical utility while remaining grounded in the reviewer concern and paper content. This analysis does not establish performance on fundamentally non-resolvable concerns such as irreparable methodological flaws or purely subjective novelty disputes. Evaluating such concerns would require different benchmark design in which abstention, rejection of the method, or multiple incompatible expert judgments can be treated as valid outcomes; we take first step in this direction in Appendix G. Held-out Evaluation of Zero-Shot Abstention G.1 Motivation and Relation to Reviewer Concerns The task formulation in Section 3.1 requires abstention: when the paper context does not support the target weakness label, the model must return no claim (k=0) rather than fabricate weakness. Because every instance in ActReview-40K and ActReview-Bench is derived from weakness that real reviewer raised, neither resource contains non-supported (weakness, paper) pairs. We therefore do not train on negative instances. Instead we evaluate abstention as held-out, zero-shot behavior: does the weakness-conditioned instruction, together with the grounding pressure introduced during training, induce correct abstention on labels the paper does not exhibit? Several properties make this meaningful test rather than an accident of prompting. First, judging whether body of text contains evidence for specific claim is capability the Qwen3-8B-Base backbone already possesses from pretraining; abstention does not require dedicated training signal. Second, the instruction if the paper has no weakness under this label, output exactly None appears in every SFT and RL prompt, so the model is repeatedly exposed to the rule even though it never sees None target. Third, both training stages push the model toward asserting only what the retrieved context supports: SFT targets are tightly grounded in retrieved chunks, and the RL rubric assigns zero reward to claims that hallucinate paper content or address the wrong label (Appendix D). Abstention is the natural endpoint of that constraint when no supporting evidence exists. The opposing force is prior toward always answering, induced by training exclusively on supported instances; whether grounding pressure overcomes that prior is an empirical question, which this evaluation answers. Wpos over the 17-label taxonomy, preferring labels whose Level-1 parent category does not appear in Wpos, since weakness type from an entirely unraised category is more likely to be genuinely absent. We target balanced distribution of roughly 20 instances per Level-2 label. Full-paper inference. For each non-supported paperlabel pair, we use the same full-paper inference protocol as in the main ActReview-Bench evaluation. The only difference between supported and non-supported instances is whether the queried weakness label is supported by the paper. Verification that the label is absent. distractor label is only valid negative if the paper truly does not exhibit that weakness. We use label-absence screening prompt adapted from the retrieval-quality protocol in Figure 11. Given the same full-paper context used for inference and the target label definition, GPT-5.4 classifies each pair as present, absent, or uncertain; only pairs classified as absent are retained. For conditional labels such as L2.7.1 (Missing Computational Cost, Runtime, and Scalability Analysis), whose taxonomy definition applies only when the paper makes claim that depends on the missing content (Appendix C.1), the prompt explicitly checks both this materiality condition and whether the corresponding content is adequately reported anywhere in the paper, including appendices, before deciding absence so that paper is not marked present merely for lacking discussion it never needed, nor for content it already reports outside the main text. The complete prompt is provided in Figure 19. The final split contains Nneg=360 operationally non-supported pairs retained after GPT-5.4 screening. As check on this screen, an author with peer-review experience inspected 29-instance random sample of the retained pairs; the human spot-check agrees with the screening decision on 27 of 29 sampled pairs (93.1%). Scope. Absent here means the full-paper context provides no evidence for the label, verified by an LLM screen and human sample; it is an operational, not exhaustive, notion. Systematically characterizing every weakness paper does not exhibit is outside the scope of this evaluation. G.3 Metrics We frame abstention as binary decision (answer vs. abstain) and report, as percentages: Answer Rate (supported): fraction of the 1,000 ActReview-Bench Task-1 instances where the model produced at least one claim. False-Abstention Rate (supported): fraction where the model returned None for reviewer-raised positive instance. This is computed on the Task-1 outputs already generated for the main experiments and requires no new inference. Abstention Rate (non-supported): fraction of the Nneg instances where the model correctly returned None. Over-generation Rate (non-supported): fraction where the model fabricated claim (1Abstention Rate). Balanced Accuracy: mean of Answer Rate and Abstention Rate. All models receive the same abstention-aware task instruction and the same input context. After stripping whitespace and formatting tokens, outputs equal to None are counted as abstentions; all other non-empty outputs are counted as answers. G.4 Results Table 25 shows that all models answer supported instances reliably: Answer Rate is at least 95%, and the FalseAbstention Rate is at most 5%, so no model abstains indiscriminately. The models diverge sharply on non-supported instances. Prompt-based and specialized review generators rarely abstain: GPT-5.1schema fabricates weakness under 68.6% of non-supported labels and DeepReviewer-14B under 87.8%, consistent with strong prior that queried label always corresponds to real problem and with the fact that generic criticism can be produced for almost any label. ACTREVIEW abstains far more often: ACTREVIEW-SFT returns None on 71.4% of non-supported instances and ACTREVIEW-RL on 78.3%, while keeping the False-Abstention Rate on supported instances at 4.6%. The gain from RL over SFT (+6.9 points of Abstention Rate) is consistent with the rubrics hard penalty on wronglabel and hallucinated claims, which rewards withholding an unsupported claim. Balanced Accuracy improves from 68.2% for the strongest evaluated non-ActReview baseline, Qwen3-32B, to 86.9% for ACTREVIEW-RL, an absolute improvement of 18.7 percentage points. ACTREVIEW-SFT and ACTREVIEW-RL exhibit substantially stronger zero-shot abstention than the evaluated baselines. Moreover, RL improves the abstention rate over SFT by 6.9 percentage points, consistent with the grounding-oriented reward design. However, ACTREVIEW-RL still over-generates on 21.7% of screened nonsupported pairs, motivating explicit negative training and evaluation on harder within-category distractors. G.5 Case Study Figure 20 presents two successful abstention cases and one representative over-generation failure. In Cases 1 and 2, ACTREVIEW-RL correctly returns None because the full-paper context shows the queried weakness does not apply, either because the paper makes no claim the label would be material to, or because the paper makes such claim but adequately supports it elsewhere in the text. In Case 3, the model incorrectly infers formatting-related weakness from the discussion of Table 7, illustrating the residual over-generation behavior reflected by the 21.7% error rate in Table 25. 36 Prompt for Weakness Segmentation You are analyzing peer review. Segment the review into individual, independent weakness points. Task: Identify all distinct weakness points, concerns, or questions raised by the reviewer. Each point should be complete, self-contained critique. Number the points sequentially as Point 1, Point 2, etc. Output format: Point 1: [First weakness] Point 2: [Second weakness] Guidelines: Merge closely related sub-points into one atomic weakness. Each point should be substantial and technically meaningful. Preserve the reviewers original wording whenever possible. Prefer content from sections such as Weaknesses, Concerns, or Questions when present. Extract only technical concerns, questions, or requests for improvement. Do not extract attitude statements, summary statements, recommendation statements, or score announcements. Do not extract any text that references rebuttal, revision, or author response. Prompt for WeaknessRebuttal Span Mapping You are analyzing peer-review discussion. Map each weakness point to the specific part of the author rebuttal that directly addresses it. Task: For each atomic weakness, identify the minimal rebuttal span that provides substantive author response. The span should directly answer, clarify, justify, or provide evidence for the corresponding weakness. Output format: W1 [Exact rebuttal text addressing W1] (Confidence: 0.95) W2 No Response (Confidence: 1.00) Critical rules: Extract exact text from the rebuttal; do not paraphrase. Map each weakness to its own most specific rebuttal segment. Prefer the shortest span that fully addresses the weakness. If weakness is not substantively addressed, write No Response. If the rebuttal quotes or restates the reviewers weakness before answering, extract only the authors reply. If the extracted segment is identical or nearly identical to the weakness text, write No Response. Assign confidence score reflecting how directly the rebuttal span addresses the weakness. Figure 7: Prompt templates used for atomic weakness segmentation and weaknessrebuttal span mapping. The first prompt decomposes full reviews into self-contained weakness units, while the second prompt aligns each weakness to the minimal author-response span that addresses it. 37 Prompt for Rebuttal-Guided Feedback Enhancement You are rewriting peer-review feedback into structured initial-review-style feedback. Input: You are given: 1. Paper metadata, including title, abstract, and keywords. 2. The target weakness category. 3. The original reviewer weakness. 4. The aligned author rebuttal span. 5. Relevant paper context chunks. Goal: Write feedback as if it appeared in the original review, before the author response was written. Use the rebuttal span only as background evidence for what revision action may address the weakness. Do not mention the rebuttal, the author response, the authors later added, in the revised paper, or any post-submission change. Required output fields: Diagnostic Claim: One sentence identifying the core paper-specific deficiency. Actionable Suggestions: Concrete revision guidance that specifies: What should be revised or added. Where the revision should appear, such as section, experiment, figure, table, claim, or method description. How the authors can implement the revision. Expected Outcome: what the revision would clarify, validate, or improve. Quality requirements: The feedback should be specific and grounded in the provided paper context. The suggestions should be useful for revision rather than merely descriptive. Avoid generic advice such as add more details unless it is accompanied by concrete implementation guidance. Do not introduce unsupported claims that are not grounded in the weakness, rebuttal span, or paper context. Return only the structured feedback. The prompt converts an original reviewer weakness and its aligned rebuttal span into initial-review-style diagnostic claims and actionable revision suggestions. 38 Figure 9: Example of constructed reviewrebuttal instance in ActReview-40K. sections.title: Retrieval Quality Screening Prompt
sections.content: You are evaluating the quality of retrieved paper chunks for actionable peer-review generation. You are given: 1. Paper metadata, including title and abstract. 2. target weakness label. 3. The reviewer-identified weakness. 4. The task type: Task 1 diagnostic claim generation or Task 2 actionable suggestion generation. 5. The retrieved paper chunks. Your task is to judge whether the retrieved chunks provide sufficient context for the given task. Do not evaluate any generated model output. Do not use or assume access to the author rebuttal. Judge only from the provided paper metadata, weakness, task definition, and retrieved chunks. Evaluation criteria. For each criterion, output pass or fail, with short explanation. Weakness-relevant evidence: Do the retrieved chunks contain paper content related to the target weakness? Specific grounding support: Are the chunks specific enough to support grounded feedback, rather than only generic or superficial keyword matches? Revision localization cues: Do the chunks indicate where or how the paper could be revised, such as method section, experiment, table, figure, claim, equation, or appendix? For Task 1, this criterion may be judged based on whether the chunks localize the diagnosed issue. For Task 2, this criterion should judge whether the chunks support concrete revision guidance. Overall sufficient context: Overall, are the retrieved chunks sufficient for the target task? Task-specific interpretation. For Task 1, focus on whether the chunks support diagnosing the target weakness. For Task 2, focus on whether the chunks support both the weakness diagnosis and actionable revision guidance. Return only valid JSON in the following format: { "weakness_relevant_evidence": { "decision": "pass/fail", "reason": "short explanation" }, "specific_grounding_support": { "decision": "pass/fail", "reason": "short explanation" }, "revision_localization_cues": { "decision": "pass/fail", "reason": "short explanation" }, "overall_sufficient_context": { "decision": "pass/fail", "reason": "short explanation" } } Figure 11: Prompt used for GPT-5.4 retrieval quality screening. The prompt evaluates retrieved chunks only and does not use rebuttal text or generated model outputs. 41 Prompt for Candidate-Aware Rubric Construction You are constructing an instance-specific reward rubric for peer-review feedback generation. Input: You are given: 1. The task type, either diagnostic-claim generation or actionable-suggestion generation. 2. Paper metadata, including title, abstract, keywords, and weakness labels. 3. The original reviewer weakness. 4. Retrieved paper context chunks. 5. pool of candidate outputs sampled from the SFT model. 6. human-written or reference-style enhanced output. 7. strong LLM-generated reference output. Goal: Construct rubric that can distinguish high-quality, paper-grounded feedback from weak, generic, unsupported, or incorrectly formatted outputs. The rubric should be specific to this paperweakness instance. It should reward outputs that correctly identify the target deficiency, ground the feedback in the provided paper context, and provide concrete revision guidance when required by the task. Hard constraints: List invalid or severely flawed behaviors. Examples include: The output addresses the wrong weakness or changes the target weakness label. The output hallucinates paper content not supported by the retrieved context. The output mentions the rebuttal, author response, revised paper, or any post-submission information. The output fails to follow the required task format. The output gives only generic advice without paper-specific grounding. Weighted soft requirements: Create set of instance-specific soft requirements. Each requirement should describe one desirable property of high-quality answer. Assign each requirement weight, and make sure the weights sum to 1.0. Soft requirements should cover dimensions such as: correctness of the diagnostic claim; grounding in retrieved paper evidence; specificity to the target weakness and paper context; localization of the relevant section, experiment, table, figure, method component, or claim; actionability of the proposed revision; completeness of the required output fields; avoidance of unsupported or overly broad suggestions. Candidate-aware calibration: Use the candidate pool to identify common failure modes. The rubric should penalize failures observed in weak candidates and reward properties demonstrated by strong candidates. Do not simply copy the reference output. Instead, abstract the qualities that make the reference output useful, grounded, and actionable. Required output format: Return structured rubric with: Hard constraints: list of invalid or severely flawed output behaviors. Soft requirements: list of weighted criteria, each with name, definition, weight, and scoring guidance. Notes: brief instance-specific reminders about what the model should focus on. Figure 12: Prompt template for candidate-aware rubric construction. The rubric is constructed offline from SFT candidates, reference-style enhanced outputs, and strong LLM-generated outputs, then frozen before reinforcement learning. 42 Prompt for Rubric Requirement Scoring You are strict but fair grader evaluating the quality of an academic peer review output. You will be given Task 1 output and single grading requirement. Task: Score how well the output satisfies the requirement using one integer from 1 to 5. Scale: 5: The requirement is fully and clearly satisfied. 4: The requirement is mostly satisfied, with only minor gaps. 3: The requirement is partially satisfied. 2: The requirement is barely satisfied. 1: The requirement is not satisfied. Important rules: Use the full 15 range when appropriate. Do not default to 3 unless the evidence is genuinely mixed. Return only single integer: 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5. Do not provide any explanation. Input format: ## Task Type Task 1 (Weakness Claim Discovery) ## Grading Requirement [Requirement from the frozen rubric] ## Review Output to Grade [Model-generated output] Score (1--5): Figure 13: Prompt used to score each weighted soft requirement in the frozen rubric. The judge returns single integer score from 1 to 5 for each requirement, which is then normalized and combined using the rubric weights. 43 Prompt for Direct Judge Reward You are an expert evaluator for academic peer-review feedback. Input: You are given: 1. Paper metadata and retrieved paper context. 2. target weakness label. 3. The task type: Task 1 or Task 2. 4. model-generated output. Goal: Evaluate the model-generated output directly. Do not use any instance-specific rubric. Do not compare the output to reference answer. Judge the output only based on the paper context, the target weakness label, and the task definition. Task definitions: Task 1: The output should contain diagnostic claims that identify concrete deficiencies in the paper under the target weakness label. Task 2: The output should contain actionable suggestions that explain what should be revised, where the revision should appear, how it can be implemented, and what outcome the revision should achieve. Scoring dimensions: Score each applicable dimension from 0 to 5. Task 1 Technical Accuracy: For Task 1 only, is the diagnostic claim factually correct, paper-grounded, and supported by the retrieved context? Penalize hallucinated paper content, unsupported criticisms, or claims that address the wrong weakness. Task 1 Overall: For Task 1 only, how useful is the output for helping authors understand the core weakness in the paper? Task 2 Actionability: For Task 2 only, does the output provide concrete what, where, how, and expectedoutcome guidance that an author can follow? Task 2 Overall: For Task 2 only, how useful is the output for helping authors revise the paper to address the target weakness? Special case: If the target weakness is not supported by the provided paper context, an output of None may receive high Task 1 technical-accuracy score. However, None should not receive high overall or actionability score unless the lack of support is clearly justified. Required output format: Return only valid JSON. For Task 1, use: { "task1_technical_accuracy": 0, "task1_overall": 0, "brief_reason": "short explanation" } For Task 2, use: { "task2_actionability": 0, "task2_overall": 0, "brief_reason": "short explanation" } Figure 14: Prompt used for the direct-judge reward ablation. Unlike our candidate-aware rubric reward, this baseline evaluates outputs using fixed task-level dimensions and does not receive an instance-specific rubric. 44 Prompt for Task 1 Pairwise Judge You are neutral expert evaluator comparing two AI-generated diagnostic claims for academic peer review. Input: You are given: 1. Paper metadata, including title and abstract. 2. target weakness label. 3. The reference claim count. 4. Assistant As generated diagnostic claims. 5. Assistant Bs generated diagnostic claims. Goal: Determine which assistant provides better diagnostic claims for the given paper and weakness label. The primary question is: which set of claims would better help authors understand the concrete weakness in the paper? Scoring dimensions: Score each assistant on each dimension using an integer from 0 to 5. Technical Accuracy: Are the claims factually correct and supported by the paper metadata and context? Penalize hallucinated paper content, unsupported criticisms, or claims that address the wrong weakness. Depth and Constructiveness: Do the claims explain why the weakness matters rather than merely restating generic concern? Specificity and Grounding: Do the claims refer to concrete paper elements, such as methods, experiments, datasets, assumptions, figures, tables, equations, or claims? Overall: Overall, how useful are the claims for helping authors understand the target weakness? Scoring guide: 5: Excellent; accurate, specific, well-grounded, and highly useful. 4: Strong; mostly accurate and useful, with only minor gaps. 3: Adequate; partially useful but missing important specificity or depth. 2: Weak; only loosely relevant or mostly generic. 1: Very poor; largely unsupported, shallow, or misaligned. 0: Fundamentally wrong, hallucinated, or not responsive to the task. Key rules: Judge semantic quality, not surface wording. Do not reward longer answer unless it adds accurate and useful content. Penalize unsupported claims, hallucinated paper content, or claims unrelated to the target weakness label. The Overall score should reflect holistic reviewer usefulness, not simply the average of the other dimensions. Output format: Return only valid JSON with integer scores from 0 to 5. Do not include reasoning. { "technical accuracy": {"score a": "depth and constructiveness": "specificity and grounding": {"score a": "overall": } 0, "score b": {"score a": {"score a": 0} 0, "score b": 0}, 0, "score b": 0, "score b": 0}, 0}, User template: Paper Title: {title} Abstract: {abstract} Weakness Label: {weakness label} Reference Claim Count: {gt count} claims Assistant As Claims: {claims a} Assistant Bs Claims: {claims b} Figure 15: LLM-as-a-judge prompt template for Task 1 pairwise evaluation. We apply the swap trick by exchanging Assistant and Assistant across two rounds, then average scores before computing the final verdict. 45 Prompt for Task 2 Pairwise Judge You are neutral expert evaluator comparing two AI-generated actionable suggestions for academic peer-review revision. Input: You are given: 1. Paper metadata, including title and abstract. 2. diagnostic claim that the suggestions should address. 3. Assistant As actionable suggestion. 4. Assistant Bs actionable suggestion. Goal: Determine which assistant provides more useful revision guidance for addressing the diagnostic claim. The primary question is: which suggestion would real author find more useful for revising the paper? Scoring dimensions: Score each assistant on each dimension using an integer from 0 to 5. Technical Accuracy: Is the suggestion technically sound and free of hallucinated paper content? Penalize unsupported claims, infeasible suggestions, or references to non-existent sections, figures, tables, or experiments. Depth and Constructiveness: Does the suggestion address the underlying weakness rather than merely restating the problem? Actionability: Does the suggestion provide concrete what, where, how, and expected-outcome guidance that an author can directly follow? Overall: Overall, how useful is the suggestion as practical revision guidance? Scoring guide: 5: Excellent; accurate, concrete, localized, and directly actionable. 4: Strong; useful and mostly concrete, with only minor gaps. 3: Adequate; partially actionable but missing important specificity. 2: Weak; mostly generic or difficult for authors to implement. 1: Very poor; vague, unsupported, or largely unhelpful. 0: Fundamentally wrong, hallucinated, or not responsive to the task. Key rules: Specific what, exact where, and step-by-step how should be preferred over longer but vague suggestions. Penalize suggestions that invent paper content or refer to unavailable evidence. Penalize suggestions that only say add more details or clarify the method without concrete implementation guidance. The Overall score should reflect holistic author usefulness, not simply the average of the other dimensions. Output format: Return only valid JSON with integer scores from 0 to 5. Do not include reasoning. { "technical accuracy": {"score a": "depth and constructiveness": "actionability": {"score a": "overall": } {"score a": 0, "score b": {"score a": 0, "score b": 0} 0, "score b": 0}, 0, "score b": 0}, 0}, User template: Paper Title: {title} Abstract: {abstract} Diagnostic Claim Being Addressed: {claim} Assistant As Actionable Suggestion: {suggestion a} Assistant Bs Actionable Suggestion: {suggestion b} Figure 16: LLM-as-a-judge prompt template for Task 2 pairwise evaluation. The swap trick and verdict computation follow the same protocol as Task 1. 46 Paper Input Title: Probing LLMs for Hate Speech Detection: Strengths and Vulnerabilities Weakness Label: L2.1.1 Insufficient or Narrow Experimental Evaluation Venue / Year: EMNLP 2023 Reference Claim Claim 1: The evaluation relies on only two large language models and three datasets, limiting the generalizability of the conclusions about LLM performance in hate-speech detection. GPT-5.1 (prompt-based) Claude-4.6 (prompt-based) Claim 1: The experimental evaluation is limited to only two proprietary LLMs (GPT-3.5 and text-davinci), without comparison to broader range of contemporary or open-source models, which restricts the generality of the conclusions. Claim 2: The paper does not compare the proposed prompting setups against strong supervised or fine-tuned baselines (e.g., state-of-the-art hate speech classifiers or LLMs with in-context learning), making it unclear how competitive the reported zero-shot improvements actually are. Claim 3: The study evaluates only on three English datasets from similar toxicity/hate domains and does not include out-of-domain, cross-lingual, or robustness/adversarial tests, so the claimed benefits of adding target and rationale information are not shown to generalize beyond these specific benchmarks. Claim 1: The study evaluates only two LLMs (GPT-3.5 and text-davinci, which are closely related OpenAI models) without including open-source models (e.g., LLaMA, Falcon) or models from other providers, severely limiting the generalizability of conclusions about LLM capabilities for hate speech detection. Claim 2: The evaluation is restricted entirely to zero-shot setting, with no comparison against few-shot prompting or fine-tuned baselines, making it impossible to contextualize whether the reported 2030% improvements are competitive with standard supervised approaches. Claim 3: The three datasets (HateXplain, Implicit Hate, ToxicSpans) are all English-language benchmarks, and the paper provides no evaluation on multilingual or cross-lingual hate speech data, leaving the scope of findings unjustifiably narrow given that hate speech is global, multilingual phenomenon. Analysis: Both GPT-5.1 and Claude-4.6 generate three claims, whereas the reference contains only one concise claim covering the core issuelimited model and dataset scope. Semantically, the generated claims are valid and grounded, but they decompose the single reference claim into finer-grained sub-issues, including open-source model coverage, zero-shot evaluation setting, and multilingual generalization. This indicates that prompt-based LLMs tend to over-generate and broaden the scope relative to the reference, which may reduce precision in downstream evaluation. Note: no reviewer raised this weakness label for this paper; you are judging directly against the paper content, not against reviewer complaint. Your task is to judge whether the paper exhibits the target weakness, based only on the provided paper content and the label definition. Do not use or assume access to the author rebuttal or to any reviewer comments. Conditional labels. If it is reported there in adequate detail, the paper does not exhibit the weakness even though the claim is made; classify the label as absent. Only classify present if the claim is made and the corresponding content is missing or inadequate everywhere in the paper. Decision. Return one of: present: the paper content provides clear evidence of the target weakness. absent: the paper content provides no evidence of the target weakness. uncertain: the paper content is ambiguous or insufficient to decide.
